output.summary: The September 15-16, 2026 minutes lean clearly hawkish. On inflation, participants said it "remained elevated and that they had not seen sufficient progress on lowering inflation in recent months"; several cited elevated core services and core goods, some saw underlying inflation above 2 percent moving sideways, and many relayed increased business cost pressures with some noting firmer pass-through. Risks were "generally assessed" as skewed to the upside, with some seeing them more skewed recently, many warning elevated energy prices could broaden pressures, several citing tariffs, and some worried about unanchoring expectations. On the labor market, a majority saw it strengthening "a bit" and participants viewed it "close to maximum employment," though several noted low dynamism and some argued aggregate wage growth was moderate (the main dovish notes). On policy, all participants backed the 1/4 point hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, several saw policy as not or only mildly restrictive, many/a number favored a higher path, and crucially "most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end." What would change minds: they stressed an "open mind" and dependence on "incoming information and its implications for the outlook and the balance of risks." Net lean for the 2026-10-28 decision is hawkish (+6 bp), driven mainly by the "most participants" expectation of a further year-end hike, tempered only by data-dependence language.

output.summary: The September 2026 minutes are strongly hawkish. All participants supported the 1/4-point hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, and 'most participants assessed that another increase in the target range for the federal funds rate would likely be appropriate by year end.' On inflation, participants saw it elevated with risks skewed to the upside ('some' saw risks more skewed recently), with 'many' citing cost pressures from energy and the AI buildout and 'several' flagging tariffs. On the labor market, a 'majority' saw recent strengthening and 'almost all' judged labor-market risks diminished and broadly balanced, though 'some' noted moderate wage growth and 'several' noted low dynamism (modest dovish offsets). 'Several' viewed policy as not restrictive or only mildly restrictive, and 'a number' viewed a higher path as necessary on modal outlooks. What would change minds: participants stressed an open mind with future decisions depending on incoming information and the balance of risks. Net lean toward the October 28 decision is clearly hawkish, hence +7.

output.summary: The minutes are decisively hawkish. Participants judged inflation remained elevated with insufficient recent progress; several cited elevated core goods inflation, some saw underlying inflation above 2 percent moving sideways, and several noted elevated short-term inflation expectations, while many cited increased business cost pressures. On the labor market, a majority saw a bit of recent strengthening near maximum employment, though several noted low dynamism and some said wages were not a source of inflation pressure. Inflation risks were generally skewed to the upside (some said increasingly so), with upside risks from energy prices, further tariffs, and the AI buildout. On policy, all backed the September hike to 3-3/4 to 4 percent, many framed a higher path as prudent risk management, several saw policy as not restrictive or only mildly restrictive, and most expected another increase by year end. The chief offsets are a few participants flagging BEA methodology softening recent PCE and some noting moderate wages. The stated mind-changer is incoming data and the balance of risks. Net lean for the 2026-10-28 decision is hawkish.

output.summary: The September 15-16, 2026 minutes read decidedly hawkish. On inflation, participants viewed it as still elevated with upside risks: several cited elevated core services and core goods price increases, some saw underlying inflation above target and moving sideways, many cited increased business cost pressures, and several flagged tariff and energy risks. On the labor market, a majority assessed it had strengthened a bit and most viewed it near maximum employment, though several noted low dynamism and some said wage growth was moderate and not inflationary. On the policy path, most participants assessed a further rate increase would likely be appropriate by year end, many emphasized risk-management grounds, and several viewed the current rate as not or only mildly restrictive. Almost all saw inflation risks tilted up while labor-market risks were balanced. On what would change their minds, participants stressed data-dependence and an open mind at each meeting. With the next decision on 2026-10-28 and 'most' participants pointing to another hike by year end, the net lean is hawkish (+6 bp), tempered only by the stated data-dependence and a minority dovish labor/wage view.
